sentences.text: Last time, we ended with a wish: one ruler for risk, where everything we know about a patient turns into a single probability.
Here's the obvious way to build it.
Start a typical patient at 20%, then add points for each risk factor.
Age 81: plus 25. Diabetes: plus 30. A third hospital stay this year: plus 35.
That's 110%.
A probability can't do that. Adding points was the wrong move, on the wrong ruler.
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: odds, and the curve that turns any patient into a probability.
Let's try a different ruler.
Take ten patients who each have a 20% chance of coming back. On average, two do, and eight don't.
Probability compares the two with all ten.
Odds compare the two with the eight: one to four, or a quarter.
At 50%, it's five against five: odds of one.
At 80%, eight against two: odds of four.
And as the probability creeps toward 100%, the odds just keep running: 9, 99, 999.
This ruler has no ceiling.
But it's a lopsided ruler.
Every patient below fifty-fifty is squeezed between zero and one, while everyone above gets all the room in the world.
The cure is a logarithm.
On a log scale, every doubling of the odds is one equal step: a quarter, a half, one, two, four.
This is the log-odds ruler. Fifty-fifty sits at zero.
20% is about minus 1.4, and 80% is plus 1.4: perfectly symmetric.
And it runs forever in both directions. No floor, no ceiling, nothing to bump into.
Here's why that matters. On the log-odds ruler, a risk factor is simply a step.
Take one that multiplies the odds by four: a step of 1.4 to the right.
Now give that same step to four different patients.
On the probability ruler, 5% becomes 17%. 20% becomes 50%. 50% becomes 80%. And 80% becomes 94%.
Same step, very different jumps: big in the middle, small near the ends.
And nobody ever goes past one hundred.
Now picture a risk factor that comes in amounts, like the number of earlier hospital stays.
Suppose each extra stay is one more equal step in log-odds.
On this scale, the pattern is a straight line. Its slope is the size of the step, and we'll call it beta.
Now switch the vertical axis back to probability.
The line bends into an S: steep in the middle, flat at both ends, and always between zero and one.
How steep it is depends on where you stand. The steepness is proportional to p times one minus p: greatest at fifty-fifty, fading to nothing at the ends.
Keep that in your pocket. It comes back when we fit the model.
Turn beta up, and the S gets steeper.
Shift the starting point, and the whole curve slides sideways.
Let's fit one of these by hand. Remember Cedar?
Ten lower-risk patients, 2 readmitted. Ten higher-risk patients, 6 readmitted.
So the odds are 2 to 8, a quarter; and 6 to 4, one and a half.
Divide one by the other, and you get an odds ratio of six. At Cedar, higher risk multiplies the odds by six.
On the log-odds ruler, that's a step of 1.79, starting from minus 1.39.
Those two numbers are a complete logistic model of Cedar.
One caution. Six times the odds is not six times the risk.
Cedar's rate went from 20% to 60%: three times, not six.
Now, back to our patient. This time, we add on the right ruler.
Each risk factor is a step in log-odds, and the steps simply stack, one after another.
And the probability? 94%.
High, but still a probability.
From now on, every chip carries its probability with it, as a shaded slice.
A sliver for a low-risk patient; nearly the whole disc for this one.
Let's gather it up.
Odds compare the patients who come back with those who don't.
Log-odds is the ruler where risk factors add.
And the S-curve carries the sum back to a probability.
So now every patient has a probability.
Add them up across a clinic, and you get a number of patients: the readmissions we should expect.
Next time, we'll set that number beside what actually happened. Observed, versus expected.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
